papers.title: Sex and generation shape the genetic architecture of smoking initiation
papers.abstract: The rapidly changing cultural contexts over the past century modified the genetic factors that influence smoking initiation (SI). Using data from nearly seven million respondents, we conducted genome-wide associations study (GWAS) meta-analyses stratified by sex and generation across European, East Asian, African American, and Latino genetic ancestry populations. Sex and generation, but not genetic ancestry, moderate both the SNP-based heritability estimates and associations with individual loci. Specifically, SI is more heritable in females and younger generations. Furthermore, the impact of both discrete policy changes that target smoking and the gradual cultural redefinition of smoking norms across sex and generation are captured within the patterns of cross-trait genetic correlations between SI and extant smoking-relevant phenotypes. Robust cross-ancestry genetic correlations allowed us to meta-analyze the results across subsamples, identifying 1,717 loci associated with SI, including both main and moderated associations for either moderator. Genome-wide heterogeneity analyses identified 45 sex-specific loci and 7 generation-specific loci with distinct associations with SI. Finemapping analyses highlighted 389 and 304 loci with distinct patterns of potential causal variants by sex and generation. Accordingly, sex- and generation-specific macrosocial contexts dynamically influence the genetic architecture of SI, underscoring the need to consider gene-environment interplay for health behaviors as societal norms evolve.

papers.title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
papers.abstract: **Background.** Rule derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce. Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration. **Methods.** We ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on *Escherichia coli* urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW. The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern). Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits. Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or prior-probability correction. These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training. Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history. UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model. Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals. **Results.** All rule-derived labels were susceptible. Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary. The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline. Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries. Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5. The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses). At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration. **Conclusions.** Under these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training. Evaluations of weak supervision should include such a baseline and should report calibration as well as discrimination. **Keywords:** weak supervision; limited-label learning; label budget; probability calibration; class imbalance; antimicrobial resistance

papers.title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. Methods: BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. Findings: We used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46.1% (95% CI 43.0-49.3) to 80.9% (78.3-83.3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a model's accuracy by up to 33.1 percentage points, leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: chain-of-thought prompting; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MedQA accuracy by up to 11.3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions. We also tested the impact of ablation on benchmarking using the MMMU benchmark dataset. Removing images lowered the accuracy by 18.0 and 19.3 points respectively for the two strongest models. Finally, the accuracy of agentic benchmarks using a sandboxed interpreter increased on computational biology tasks by 36-63 points. Interpretation: Benchmarking is essential to assess the impact and validity of LLMs for medical applications. BenchmarkHub allows a fair and rigorous comparison of models across established datasets, including the possibility to upload their own datasets. The suite includes visual tools to ease model comparison and ranking without any programming knowledge. Self-hosted infrastructure that records every choice and parameter makes benchmark claims checkable without data leaving the institution.

papers.title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop
papers.abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.

papers.title: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification
papers.abstract: Background: Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings. Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors. Methods: We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification. An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates. Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks. The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments. Results: In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline. Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858. External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409. Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC. Conclusions: Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline. Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations. The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.

papers.title: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation
papers.abstract: ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-ExperimentAssay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccinerelated study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

papers.title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes
papers.abstract: Objective Negative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institution's data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. Methods Four LLM agents operate on an institution's Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospital's electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. Results MENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was {kappa}=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. Conclusion Combining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone. Restricting reasoning to discordant candidates kept computation time below 40% of that with reasoning in all agents. Every decision comes with its evidence and rationale for investigators' final review.

papers.title: Assessment of Undergraduate Psychological Wellbeing Using Explainable Machine Learning: A Study from Sri Lanka
papers.abstract: Academic, psychosocial, financial, environmental, and interpersonal factors are widely recognized as important contributors to the overall wellbeing of students. This study aimed to identify factors associated with the psychological wellbeing of university undergraduates and compare the performance of machine learning models for binary and multiclass classification of wellbeing status using self-reported survey data from undergraduates at the University of Peradeniya, Sri Lanka. The findings may facilitate the early identification of students with lower wellbeing and inform targeted interventions to foster a healthier and more supportive academic environment. Cross-sectional questionnaire data from 2,913 undergraduates were analyzed to classify psychological wellbeing using overall happiness scores. Scores were grouped into binary (1-5 and 6-9) and multiclass (1-4, 5-6, and 7-9) categories. Data preprocessing included missing value imputation, one-hot encoding, and feature scaling where appropriate. Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models were trained using repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation and evaluated using macro F1-score, ROC-AUC, and classification reports. SHAP analysis was employed to interpret feature contributions and enhance model interpretability. XGB achieved the highest macro-F1 score (70.5%) for binary classification, with a test accuracy of 72.5%. The model correctly classified 63.6% and 80% of participants in the lower and higher psychological wellbeing groups, respectively. For multiclass classification, RF achieved the highest macro-F1 score (54.6%), with a test accuracy of 56.5%. The model correctly classified 48%, 57%, and 60% of participants in the lower, intermediate, and higher psychological wellbeing groups, respectively. SHAP analysis identified academic coping, health and wellbeing, financial circumstances, and interpersonal relationships as key predictors of psychological wellbeing across both models. These findings demonstrate the potential of machine learning to classify psychological wellbeing groups using self-reported data, supporting early identification of students at risk of poor wellbeing and informing targeted university-level mental health interventions.

papers.title: Detecting Contradictory Evidence on Drug-Disease Associations at Scale
papers.abstract: Contradictory claims about drug efficacy across randomized controlled trials (RCTs) complicate evidence-based medicine, yet existing automated methods classify isolated sentence pairs and do not explain why studies disagree. We present DrugCon, a large language model (LLM)-based framework that extracts study conclusions from RCT abstracts, links these claims when they concern the same drug-disease association, detects contradictions with counterfactual reasoning, and explains them using a taxonomy of ten study-level factors such as population, dosage, and outcome measures. Applying DrugCon to 224,756 RCT abstracts, we built DrugCon-Bench, an exhaustively annotated benchmark of 542 contradictory claim pairs from 819 abstracts. Most contradictions involve more than one study-level factor (75.5%). The most common are differences in outcome measures (64.0%), populations (51.3%), and dosage or exposure duration (35.6%). DrugCon achieves an F1 score of 0.744 for contradiction detection, outperforming rule-based, supervised, and natural language inference baselines, and an F1 of 0.482 for identifying explanatory study factors. DrugCon enables scalable and explainable analysis of contradictory clinical evidence.

papers.title: Network scaling in swarm learning across real hospitals of different sizes: a KPI-driven analysis on the eICU Collaborative Research Database
papers.abstract: Background. Distributed learning lets hospitals train prediction models jointly without exchanging patient records, but how the benefits of a swarm network change as it grows, and which hospitals gain most, have so far been studied with artificial partitions of single-center databases. We examined network scaling on real hospitals that differ in size, volume and sepsis prevalence. Methods. We applied the seven-KPI swarm-learning evaluation framework (Swarm Gain, Local Gain, Relative Local Gain, Model Stability Index, Jain's index, Data Utility Index and label entropy) to progressive network scaling on the eICU Collaborative Research Database. From 25 hospitals (71,887 ICU stays; sepsis prevalence 16.6%), six hospitals stratified by bed size (two small, two medium, two large; 14,776 stays) formed networks of two, four and six hospitals in all six category-joining orders; four further hospitals served as substitutes in robustness checks. Swarm learning was simulated with the client-controlled workflow of NVIDIA FLARE (federated averaging, 30 rounds, five random seeds). The task was whole-stay sepsis classification from discretized vital-sign, laboratory and medication features with a 1,313-parameter feedforward network, with AUROC as the metric. Results. Network AUROC increased with every addition in every ordering, from 0.734 (small-first), 0.755 (medium-first) and 0.781 (large-first) at two hospitals to 0.804 (SD 0.002) at six. Swarm Gain exceeded 1 at all nine unique transitions (mean 1.042 for two-to-four and 1.020 for four-to-six hospitals). Every hospital had Local Gain below 1; relative improvement over local training ranged from 4.1% for the strongest hospital (local AUROC 0.773) to 29.5% for the weakest (0.621), averaging 25.5% for small and 5.9% for large hospitals. Adding large hospitals gave existing members the largest gain (mean Relative Local Gain +6.2%); adding small hospitals never reduced it. Seed-to-seed variability fell from a coefficient of variation of 2.2% at two hospitals to 0.2% at six. Feature distributions were near-identical across hospitals (Data Utility Index 0.005-0.013), whereas the change in label entropy tracked Swarm Gain (r = 0.74). Substituting alternative medium or large hospitals left network AUROC between 0.790 and 0.805. Conclusions. On real multi-hospital data, swarm participation improved every hospital's model, most for hospitals with the weakest local models, with no transition in which an addition harmed the network. Because all orderings end in the same six-hospital network, joining order affected only intermediate performance. The results characterize the KPI framework under real inter-hospital variation in volume and label prevalence and support inclusive recruitment anchored by large hospitals. Per-hospital evaluation and warm-started sequential joining are needed to quantify member-level effects.

papers.title: Beyond one-off training: Continuing support, system stability and worker-borne costs shape electronic community health reporting in Kisii County, Kenya
papers.abstract: Kenya's electronic community health information system (eCHIS) moves household and service data from community health promoters' phones into the national health information system. When reporting quality falls short, the usual response is more training and competency frameworks. We tested whether user capability and one-off training explain how well the system performs for its users, or whether continuing support and system stability matter more. We also examined where along the reporting chain quality was lost. In this convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study in Kisii County, we surveyed 343 eCHIS users in 22 facility catchments, observed five sites against a structured checklist, and interviewed 13 key informants. Hierarchical ordinal and logistic regression with facility-clustered standard errors modelled user satisfaction and perceived system consistency. Formal eCHIS training was near universal (94.5%) and was not associated with either outcome. Adding continuing support (refresher training, mentorship and technical support response time) significantly improved both models. McFadden's pseudo-R{superscript 2} for consistency rose from 0.06 to 0.16. Each faster level of technical support response almost doubled the odds of reporting a consistent system (adjusted odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.35-2.58). Each step up in crash frequency reduced the odds of higher satisfaction (0.60, 0.43-0.84). Digital comfort remained independently associated with both outcomes. At the observation sites, form logic secured completeness (all required fields were filled at 5 of 5 sites), but timeliness (2 of 5), consistency over time (1 of 5) and use of reports for decisions (0 of 4) failed, mostly because of synchronisation. In open-ended responses, 43.4% of respondents raised the cost of data bundles. Informants described promoters paying for connectivity and reinstalling the failing application themselves. Reporting quality depended less on what users knew than on the support around them. Competency frameworks will need matching standards for connectivity financing, support response and synchronisation monitoring.

papers.title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining
papers.abstract: Objective: To develop and evaluate AToP (Attribution to Temporal Patterns), a post-hoc explainability framework that converts per-token Integrated Gradients (IG) from a Transformer into structured temporal pattern narratives. Materials and Methods: AToP was applied to a single-stream Transformer trained on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (218,196 patients; 12.6% unplanned 30-day readmission). It mines frequent episodes from salient-token subsequences in the training cohort, aggregates attribution among patients whose records contain each token or pattern, and collapses near-duplicates by patient overlap. Validation used masking, reversed-order analysis, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison. Results: The Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34. Population-weighted attribution emphasized high-prevalence codes with small per-patient impact. Carrier-conditional attribution, the mean among patients with the token, surfaced rare high-attribution psychiatric markers including psychosis, self-harm overdose, suicidal ideation (SI), and severe major depressive disorder (MDD). Pattern-level attribution identified within-visit co-occurrences and cross-visit trajectories not captured by token rankings. Risk-increasing patterns included psychiatric sequences ({MDD, SI} [->] SI) and oncologic progressions (cancer anemia [->] ascites). Obstetric and chest pain evaluation patterns were associated with lower predicted readmission. Discussion: The framework provides two complementary views of model predictions: carrier-conditional aggregation highlights rare, highly attributed clinical features, while temporal pattern analysis identifies within-visit combinations and cross-visit trajectories missed by token-level rankings. Masking and visit-order reversal provided evidence of correspondence with model behavior, but pattern attributions do not represent unique effects or establish clinical validity. Conclusion: AToP turns a Transformer's attributions into visit-anchored temporal pattern narratives, showing which events, in which order, contribute to its readmission predictions.

papers.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
papers.abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

papers.title: Routine health information system data quality in a hill and mountain district of Nepal: a cross-sectional desk review of four years of DHIS2 data from Sankhuwasabha, 2021-2025
papers.abstract: IntroductionNepals routine health information system runs on DHIS2, but no published data-quality assessment covers its mountainous districts. The method raises a second issue: the WHO Data Quality Review (DQR) tests internal consistency partly through related-indicator pairs, assuming each indicator is recorded independently. DHIS2 validation rules act on paired values at entry, so a rule-governed pair may agree for reasons unrelated to recording quality. MethodsIn this study, a WHO DQR Module 1 desk review was conducted on aggregated DHIS2 data from all 132 facilities in Sankhuwasabha district, analysed at district and local level (palika) resolution: seven datasets for completeness and timeliness, and 17 tracer indicators for internal consistency, for fiscal year 2081/82 (2024/25) against the three preceding years (2021/22 to 2023/24). Pairs were classified in advance as rule-governed or free, and three denominator-free ratios compared with Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) 2022 estimates for Koshi Province. ResultsCompleteness was at least 90.6% in every dataset and unit. Timeliness fell below 90% in 22 of 70 unit-dataset combinations, concentrated in four remote local levels. Of four rule-governed pairs only iron and deworming changed materially, 1.42 to 1.00; two never agreed, indicating rules that query rather than block entry. The free pairs diverged: Penta-1 to Penta-3 dropout fell from +3.6% to -5.4%, negative in 9 of 10 local levels, and BCG was below Penta-1 in 8 of 10. District totals were inverted at both steps (BCG 1,537, Penta-1 1,666, Penta-3 1,756), which redistribution cannot produce. ConclusionReporting is nearly complete, but the data carry a persistent immunization anomaly that completeness and timeliness miss, pointing to a systematic recording process. Because a rule-governed pair may agree by configuration, DHIS2 assessments should classify pairs against the active validation-rule set before interpretation.

papers.title: Natural-language cohort queries on a hospital data platform: accuracy and provenance in a real-world evaluation
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccessing routinely collected clinical data for research remains technically demanding across heterogeneous hospital systems. This proof-of-concept study aimed to evaluate the accuracy and query-level traceability of a commercial natural-language (NL) data-query platform implemented at a university hospital. MethodsAn on-premises data integration platform with an NL query interface (AIRE; Briya, Tel Aviv, Israel) was connected to the institutional health data platform across three tertiary-care hospitals under an approved pseudonymization and governance framework. Implementation comprised regulatory and governance approval, and IT deployment. Twenty-five NL prompts addressing cohort identification and characterization in an adult ICD-10 C71-coded brain-tumor cohort (n = 1,594) were evaluated against manually written reference SQL and checked for a corresponding executed query in the exported log. Responses were classified into five categories. Prompts with unanswered or incorrect responses were re-posed in a new thread. ResultsThe platform was implemented over two years. Fifteen of 25 responses were exact (n = 11), concordant after definition alignment (n = 1), or incorrect but traceable from the logged SQL (n = 3); six were plausible but incorrect without a logged query, and four remained unanswered. No incorrect unlogged result recurred in a new thread. Across the initial and repeat evaluations, 22 of 23 logged responses were correct or traceable, whereas all eight unlogged responses were incorrect. ConclusionsImplementation was feasible but required substantial local institutional preparation. The NL interface reproduced SQL-derived results when definitions were explicit, while query-level provenance and verification of the displayed result were critical for identifying unreliable outputs.

papers.title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
papers.abstract: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To over-come these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients [1], we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN [2]) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves pre-processing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

papers.title: User-Informed Design of a Psychological Support Social Pet Robot for Community-Dwelling People With Long-Term Physical Disabilities: A Formative Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCommunity-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities may experience pain that interferes with daily and social activities and is associated with poorer mental wellbeing. A home-based psychological support social pet robot could offer mood check-ins, companionship, supportive interaction, and mindfulness guidance for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities. Preliminary evidence is needed to understand their preferences and translate them into candidate design requirements. ObjectiveThis study aimed to identify preliminary needs and preferences to inform a psychological support social pet robot for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities, offering mood check-ins, companionship, and mindfulness guidance at home. MethodsWe conducted a 3-phase formative user-informed design study comprising initial concept development, qualitative target user interviews, and a design workshop. Six community-dwelling adults with long-term physical disabilities took part in the interviews, and one participant also answered the workshop questions by telephone. Four authors used modified workshop materials to synthesize the interview findings and separate responses into an early product plan. ResultsQualitative content analysis of the interview transcripts produced 5 themes. These were emotional support, soft touch and appearance, mindfulness delivery, context of use, and ease of use and accessibility. Participants expressed preferences about companionship, touch, use settings, and interaction effort. The author workshop combined these findings with author and technical judgments to develop candidate requirements for dialogue and mindfulness delivery. The resulting psychological support concept combined mood check-ins and companion-oriented interaction with flexible mindfulness guidance. The design also needed to consider pain and daily routines. After the workshop, the authors developed a physical proof-of-concept prototype. It implemented only part of the candidate requirements and included additional author or technical choices. ConclusionsFor this small community-dwelling sample, target user input showed that home use, physical access, companionship, and flexible support were important. Mindfulness was one component of the broader psychological support role, alongside mood check-ins and optional companion interaction. The prototype illustrates but does not validate the early requirements. Further studies should include people with a wider range of long-term physical disabilities and test usability, accessibility, privacy, and nursing value.

papers.title: Room-Aware Transformer for Activities of Daily Living Recognition in Adults with Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Using Ambient Sensors: Development and Evaluation Study
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSUnobtrusive recognition of activities of daily living (ADLs) from ambient sensors may support longitudinal assessment of everyday functioning in adults with mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD). However, real-world activity recognition is complicated by heterogeneous home layouts, sensor configurations, routines, and class distributions. ObjectiveThis study evaluated whether a room-aware Transformer that preserves location-specific sensor structure improves participant-level ADL recognition relative to a global Transformer and a stacked unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network. MethodsFollowing pilot feasibility testing with two adult volunteers, we analyzed five homes of adults with mild NCD, comprising 92,765 minute-level observations across 67 annotated home-days. Motion, temperature, illuminance, humidity, and door-contact data were aligned to participant activity logs. The original labels were harmonized into eight categories. Models were developed separately for each home using 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows. Complete calendar days were assigned to mutually exclusive training, validation, and chronological test sets, and no sequence crossed a day or partition boundary. The same partitions and evaluation procedures were used for all three architectures. Performance was assessed on held-out test days using accuracy, per-class F1 score, and micro- and macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). ResultsThe room-aware Transformer achieved the highest or tied accuracy in 9 of 15 home-window comparisons. Its accuracy ranged from 0.27 to 0.57, micro-AUC from 0.57 to 0.82, and macro-AUC from 0.54 to 0.78. Across the 15 settings, mean accuracy was similar for the room-aware and global Transformers and higher than for the LSTM. Mean micro-AUC and macro-AUC were marginally higher for the global Transformer than for the room-aware Transformer. The room-aware model showed its clearest gains in selected contexts, including Homes C and E at 10 minutes and Home A at 60 minutes, but no architecture or temporal window was uniformly optimal. Sleep/Rest was the most consistently recognized activity, whereas low-support activities frequently had low F1 scores despite moderate or high AUC values. ConclusionsRoom-specific feature processing provided context-dependent gains in participant-level ADL classification, particularly for accuracy in several home-window settings. The marked variation across homes, activities, and temporal windows supports personalized model development, class-sensitive evaluation, and validation in larger and more diverse residential samples before clinical use.

papers.title: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
papers.abstract: BackgroundAmbient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. ObjectiveTo compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc.s ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. MethodsTwo-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and disseminationDetermined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. No patient-level data are collected. Findings will directly inform operational decision making and will be published regardless of direction.

papers.title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
papers.abstract: PURPOSETo develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODSA retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were initially performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was then trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. A dedicated intermediate model was developed to distinguish the vertebral artery from the surrounding vertebral venous plexus. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTSThe final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSIONThis study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous drainage. Summary StatementAn automated nnU-Net-based MRI pipeline enabled segmentation and three-dimensional visualization of the cranio-cervical venous system, reducing manual correction time less than 10 minutes per case. Key Points- A dedicated nnU-Net v2-based pipeline was developed for MRI-based segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system - Iterative model optimization reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours to less than 10 minutes per case. - The pipeline enabled patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions and was integrated into a dedicated software environment for visualization and analyzis.

papers.title: OPEN: A Community-Informed Metadata Framework for Interoperable Computable Phenotypes
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo identify community-prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and MethodsWe combined an international, library-led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. ResultsThe library-led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API-mediated mapping achieving 63-76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community-identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. DiscussionThrough a consensus-based, community-driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. ConclusionOPEN provides a credible, community-informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDMany transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODSWe curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTSPhysicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorffs 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSIONMulti-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

papers.title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWClinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

papers.title: Accelerometer Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering for Gait Analytics
papers.abstract: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond. Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies. This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data. Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations. Gender classification served as a proof- of-concept downstream analysis. Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information. Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0. Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations. Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established. These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features. The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations. Author SummarySensors in smartphones and wearables such as smartwatches and fitness trackers enable background recording of human walking behaviour in everyday life. This data can be used in a range of health-related applications and research, both in the fitness and in the medical domain. In order to develop robust analytical methods and applications, large and diverse datasets are desirable. However, data recorded for such purposes often differ in sensor placement, hardware specification, recording procedures, and data structure, impeding the compilation of composed datasets. In this study, we develop a harmonization framework that organizes and processes accelerometer-based gait data in a standardized way. This includes a database structure, automated gait-cycle extraction, quality-control procedures, and feature-extraction methods that can be readily applied across multiple source datasets. Using six publicly available datasets, we demonstrate the technical feasibility of our approach. A subsequent downstream analysis highlights the possibilities and limits of this approach and demonstrates where differences between datasets cannot be harmonized but need to be taken into account in subsequent analyses. By providing the framework as an open-source resource, we aim to facilitate future efforts to unlock the power of large gait datasets and therewith support reproducible gait research.

papers.title: Methodological Adherence, Reporting Completeness, and Risk of Bias in AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews: A Matched Meta-Research Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI-assisted reviews is limited. ObjectiveTo compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI assistance and matched reviews with no reported AI use, and to assess AI-use transparency. MethodsWe conducted a matched-cohort meta-research study of English-language, peer-reviewed health systematic reviews. AI-assisted reviews published during 2023-2025 were matched 1:2 to reviews with no reported AI use using individualized MEDLINE searches targeting publication timing, clinical domain, review type, and meta-analysis status. When more than two eligible comparators were available, two were randomly selected. AI assistance was defined as reported use during searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, evidence synthesis, or substantive drafting. Full texts and supplementary materials were examined to classify reported AI use. The primary outcome was a prespecified modified 13-item AMSTAR-2 methodological-adherence score (range 0-13; noninferiority margin -1 point). Secondary outcomes included PRISMA 2020 reporting completeness and ROBIS risk of bias; AI-use transparency was assessed descriptively. Adapted 13-item AMSTAR-2 confidence categories were summarized descriptively, while critical- and noncritical-domain adherence was examined in exploratory adjusted analyses. Multivariable regression models adjusted for journal impact tier, funding reporting, formal review-group affiliation, review-team size, and review-question type, using cluster-robust standard errors by matched set. Sensitivity analyses included matched-set fixed-effects models. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q5JRW). ResultsThe cohort included 231 systematic reviews: 77 AI-assisted and 154 with no reported AI use. Mean 13-item AMSTAR-2 scores were 7.58 and 9.63, respectively. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, AI-assisted reviews scored 1.64 points lower (95% CI -2.37 to -0.91); noninferiority was not demonstrated. PRISMA adherence was estimated to be 4.7 percentage points lower among AI-assisted reviews in primary adjusted analyses (95% CI -8.9 to -0.6) and 6.4 points lower in matched-set fixed-effects analyses (95% CI -10.7 to -2.1). Among reviews with assessable ROBIS ratings, 75.0% of AI-assisted reviews and 65.6% of comparators were rated low risk (adjusted difference +17.8 percentage points; 95% CI 2.7 to 33.0). Among AI-assisted reviews, model version or date was reported in 42.9%, prompts or parameters in 55.8%, and data-governance or ethics considerations in 9.1%. ConclusionsReviews reporting AI assistance had lower methodological-adherence scores and had less complete reporting, despite more favorable risk-of-bias ratings. These findings provide an early warning that AI-assisted systematic reviews may require stronger safeguards, human verification, and transparency to support trust.

papers.title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

papers.title: A Cross-Dataset Audit of Discrimination and Conformal Prediction Coverage in Keystroke-Based Parkinson's Disease Classi cation
papers.abstract: Typing dynamics are being investigated as a digital behavioral marker for Parkinsons disease (PD), but the cross-dataset reliability of typing-based classifiers remains uncertain. We evaluated four public datasets (475 participants; 270 with PD and 205 controls) across 12 transfer directions using split conformal prediction targeting 90% marginal coverage. In all three primary directions, coverage was below the 0.90 target and the one-sided tests remained significant after Holm correction: 0.598 (95% CI, 0.483-0.704) for Tappy[->]MIT, 0.850 (0.788-0.899) for MIT[->]Tappy, and 0.732 (0.684-0.777) for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Discrimination and coverage did not consistently change together: LightGBM had lower AUC than logistic regression in all 12 directions but higher coverage in 11, with larger prediction sets. Class-conditional coverage varied by target cohort: PD-conditional coverage was 0.214 for Tappy[->]MIT, whereas healthy-control coverage was 0.700 for MIT[->]Tappy and 0.627 for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Recalibration with 9 and 18 labeled target participants raised the lower confidence bound above 0.80 in the latter two directions; in Tappy[->]MIT, it remained below 0.80 even with 25 labels. Weighted conformal prediction yielded coverage of 0.918-1.000 without target labels but returned the full label set for 86%-100% of participants. Stress tests did not reproduce the observed coverage patterns, and black-box shift estimation did not support pure label shift as the dominant explanation for Tappy[->]MIT. Evaluating typing dynamics as a digital marker for PD requires cross-dataset assessment of discrimination, marginal and class-conditional coverage, and recovery costs. Clinical screening utility has not been established.

papers.title: An explainable, bias-audited machine learning model to detect hidden hepatitis C from region-wide real-world health records
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and MethodsWe conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee [≥]60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded [≥]30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. ResultsIn the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. ConclusionAn explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

papers.title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
papers.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation. Author summaryClinical studies often publish survival graphs without sharing the underlying patient records. Researchers can estimate event and follow-up times from these graphs and use them to combine evidence across studies. Artificial intelligence may reduce the work involved, but its accuracy can depend on how a figure is supplied. We studied whether an original vector PDF and a matching image led the same artificial intelligence system to reconstruct different data. Using simulated studies allowed us to compare every reconstruction with known records. The system could write and run computer code. It recovered curves more accurately from vector PDFs, which preserved readable curve coordinates, than from images containing only pixels. However, average differences in treatment estimates were small. Lower-resolution and compressed images produced larger errors, and putting an image inside a PDF did not recover the lost information. Our findings support preserving original vector figures when possible. Even when reconstructed KM curves closely matched the originals, the reconstructed data sometimes contained incorrect event counts. The results apply to one computational workflow using clean simulated figures; performance with published clinical figures, other systems, and consistently enforced revision limits still needs evaluation. Data availability statementAll data used in this study were simulated. The project repository is https://github.com/ FionaShiyinLi/km-curve-reconstruction-study. The reproducibility materials comprise reference records, input figures, reconstructed records, dataset-level results, reconstruction instructions, random seeds, and generation, reconstruction, and analysis code.

papers.title: Deep learning screening of otoscopic images for ENT referral: development, validation and deployment of NHREF OtoScan
papers.abstract: BackgroundMiddle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed-set classification rather than the referral decision a non-specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near-duplicate controls that video-derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. MethodsWe merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field-of-view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video-derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine-tuned from block_9_expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature-scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. ResultsOn the 718 held-out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1-98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4-80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8-99.6% and 66.0-83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve-class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low-confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases. Recall was consistently highest on the largest source dataset and fell on the other two, for example acute otitis media 95.5% on source A versus 50.0% on source B. ConclusionsA compact, calibrated model run on ordinary CPU hardware achieved the pre-specified 97% referral sensitivity with clinically interpretable failure modes. The source-stratified gap, and an earlier perceptual-hash split that inflated scores until it was corrected, indicate that headline accuracy in this field is strongly dependent on leakage control and acquisition style. The system is deployed with mandatory specialist review, a daily backtest and approval-gated retraining, so that prospective performance on local equipment is measured rather than assumed. It is research software and not a medical device. RegistrationNot applicable. This was retrospective model development on public data. FundingFunded by the Nawaloka Hospitals Research and Education Foundation.
